content: The recommendations address the use of the aluminum hydroxide-adsorbed, cell-free anthrax vaccine (Anthrax Vaccine Adsorbed, AVA) produced by BioPort Corporation in Lansing, Michigan, for protection against anthrax caused by Bacillus anthracis. Additionally, they include information on the use of chemoprophylaxis against B. anthracis. Anthrax is a zoonotic disease caused by the spore-forming bacterium Bacillus anthracis. It primarily affects herbivorous animals such as cattle, sheep, goats, camels, and antelope. Humans can contract anthrax through exposure to infected animals, their tissues, or direct contact with B. anthracis spores. The disease manifests in three forms depending on the route of infection: cutaneous, gastrointestinal, and inhalation. B. anthracis spores can remain viable in soil for years, posing a risk to grazing livestock but generally not to humans unless there is direct exposure. Humans can become infected through skin contact, ingestion, or inhalation of spores from contaminated animal products. Cutaneous anthrax results from direct skin contact with contaminated materials, while gastrointestinal anthrax occurs after consuming undercooked or raw infected meat. Inhalation anthrax can result from aerosolized spores during industrial processing of contaminated animal products. Person-to-person transmission of inhalation anthrax has not been documented. Globally, anthrax is most common in agricultural regions with inadequate livestock control programs. In these areas, the disease primarily affects domestic animals, which can directly or indirectly infect humans. Over 95% of human anthrax cases are cutaneous. Regions with high anthrax prevalence include South and Central America, Southern and Eastern Europe, Asia, Africa, the Caribbean, and the Middle East. In the United States, the annual incidence of human anthrax has significantly declined from approximately 130 cases in the early 1900s to no cases reported between 1993 and 2000. The last confirmed human anthrax case in the U.S. was a cutaneous case in 1992. Most U.S. cases have been cutaneous, with only 18 inhalation anthrax cases reported in the 20th century, the most recent in 1976. No gastrointestinal anthrax cases have been reported in the U.S. Anthrax has also been developed as a biological warfare agent due to the stability of B. anthracis spores, their ability to be transmitted via the respiratory route, and the high mortality rate of inhalation anthrax. The World Health Organization estimated that releasing 50 kg of B. anthracis spores upwind of a population of 500,000 could result in 95,000 deaths and 125,000 hospitalizations. The infectious dose of B. anthracis in humans is not precisely known, but studies in primates suggest that inhaling 8,000–50,000 spores can cause inhalation anthrax. The incubation period for inhalation anthrax varies and may be prolonged by post-exposure chemoprophylaxis. The pathogenesis of B. anthracis involves evasion of the immune system through an antiphagocytic capsule and the production of three proteins—protective antigen (PA), lethal factor (LF), and edema factor (EF)—that form two exotoxins: lethal toxin and edema toxin. These toxins contribute to local necrosis, extensive edema, and systemic effects such as toxemia and bacteremia. Inhaled spores can reside in alveolar recesses for weeks before being taken up by macrophages, where they germinate and replicate. Antibiotics are effective against germinating or vegetative B. anthracis but not against spores, necessitating prolonged antibiotic therapy to prevent disease development. Cutaneous anthrax, the most common form, begins as a painless papule that progresses to a vesicle and then a necrotic ulcer with a black eschar. Without antibiotics, the case-fatality rate is 20%, but with treatment, it is less than 1%. Gastrointestinal anthrax, caused by consuming contaminated meat, presents with acute inflammation of the intestinal tract, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, and bloody diarrhea. The case-fatality rate is estimated at 25%–60%. Inhalation anthrax, the most severe form, progresses from mild symptoms such as fever and muscle aches to severe respiratory distress and shock. The case-fatality rate is high, with estimates of 86%–97% in historical outbreaks. Control and prevention of anthrax involve livestock vaccination programs, rapid case detection, and proper disposal of infected animal carcasses. Human infection is controlled by reducing livestock infections, veterinary supervision of slaughter practices, and restricting imports of hides and wool from endemic regions. Vaccination of livestock with live attenuated vaccines has been effective, but these vaccines are unsuitable for humans. The human anthrax vaccine, AVA, is a cell-free filtrate of B. anthracis culture adsorbed to aluminum hydroxide. The vaccine is administered in a six-dose primary series with annual boosters. Studies are ongoing to evaluate alternative vaccination schedules and routes of administration. The efficacy of AVA is supported by animal studies, a controlled human vaccine trial, and immunogenicity data. In a clinical trial among mill workers, the vaccine demonstrated 92.5% efficacy against anthrax. However, the duration of vaccine-induced immunity in humans is unknown. Adverse events associated with AVA are generally mild and localized, with severe reactions occurring in less than 1% of cases. Post-licensure surveillance has not identified any patterns of serious adverse events clearly associated with the vaccine, except for injection-site reactions.
